extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century public and aspiring periodical essayists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and publishing short moral/literary periodical essays in the Spectator tradition, covering authorial persona and tone, attribution of help, methods for improving discourse, and moral standards (sincerity, ambition, cultivation of talent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Feigned Persona vs Authorial Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing in a feigned character (the Spectator) the author may express contempt, extol performance, or assume mock-authority without giving offence; when writing in his own name he must address readers 'in a more submissive manner, and with a just Gratitude'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licence allowable to a feigned character can cover self-praise and mock-authority; but when publishing under one's own name avoid arrogance — adapt tone to the authorial identity and be mindful of how direct statements will be received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and Acknowledgment of Assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Be candid and sincere about contributions: acknowledge papers and passages given by friends or received by letter; list names of assistants 'in the Order wherein I received the Obligation' rather than claiming undeserved praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark pieces contributed by others, publicly attribute material (even if authors did not intend to be known), and prefer honesty over retaining undeserved credit; include provenance markers where useful (e.g., letters, initials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practices to Improve Public Speaking and Discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical methods for gaining facility in speech: read aloud in private, practice calling a coach in the street, speak in chorus with others, frequent coffee-houses, take contrary opinions for exercise, and converse with women and other groups to gain freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate, varied practice (aloud reading, public banter, arguing for exercise) is recommended to overcome taciturnity and develop eloquence; seek environments that force adaptation and habit-formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for Truth and Sincerity; Avoid Partisan Factionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The author declares he is 'of no Faction', 'a Friend to no Interests but those of Truth and Virtue, nor a Foe to any but those of Vice and Folly' and will 'speak always in Truth and Sincerity of Heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodical writers should avoid inflaming party divisions; prioritize truth, virtue, and impartial moral criticism rather than serving Whig or Tory interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness and Sincerity over Polished Compliment
rubrics_metrics.description: The old English plainness and sincerity is praised; conversely, 'The Dialect of Conversation is now-a-days so swelled with Vanity and Compliment' — false politeness is condemned as making truth seem barbarous and falsehood polite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plain, honest speech in conversation and writing; avoid the fashionable excess of compliments and insincere flattery that mask real meaning (as illustrated by the Bantam ambassador's letter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate Subgenres Within an Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting is not one homogeneous art: 'it is enough if any one succeed in painting Faces, History, Battels, Landscapes, Sea-Pieces, Fruit, Flowers, or Drolls, &c.' No man is excellent in all branches, and nations may excel in different kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or practising an art, treat its branches separately — do not award a blanket superiority for one branch to justify excellence across the whole art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Where the Specific Branch Excels
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspiring practitioners should go to the place where a particular kind of painting is in greatest perfection: e.g., 'one that designs for Portrait-Painting ought to study in England' while other branches have other centres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose training and models based on the regional or institutional centers of excellence for the precise sub-discipline you wish to master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources and Patronage as Determinants of Artistic Excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence in a branch is fostered by available models and encouragement: England's abundance of 'Beautiful and noble Faces' and the wealth and generosity of the nation make it pre-eminent in face-painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and cultivate art where there are adequate subjects, exemplars, collections, and patronage — material and social conditions matter to the development of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition (Desire for Glory) as an Engine of Excellence (with Caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural passion for glory is 'one of the strongest Incitements to excel' and is 'a Spring implanted by Nature to give Motion to all the latent Powers of the Soul', though it 'may be faulty in the Excess of it'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ambition as a legitimate motivator to cultivate talent and produce work, but beware excess that leads to vanity or requests to 'exceed the Bounds of Truth' (e.g., Cicero's behaviour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Every Soul Can Excel in Something — Cultivate Particular Talents
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxim: 'though all are not capable of shining in Learning or the Politer Arts; yet every one is capable of excelling in something' — the soul 'has in this Respect a certain vegetative Power'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage finding and cultivating a particular domain of aptitude rather than assuming universal capacity; without cultivation, natural talent lies 'like a Jewel in the Mine' or produces 'Weeds or Flowers of a wilder Growth'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial Humility and Gratitude to Readers
rubrics_metrics.description: When the author writes in his own name he must show thankfulness for the public reception: he 'addresses my self to my Readers in a more submissive manner, and with a just Gratitude' and 'humbly beseech[s] the Continuance of this Inclination to favour what I may hereafter produce.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a humble, grateful tone toward readers when signing work personally; recognize public support and avoid presumptuous claims of entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent Disclosure of Publication Practices and Contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain editorial marks and provenance ('All the Papers marked with a C, an L, an I, or an O... were given me by the Gentleman...') and inform readers where assistance came from and which volumes are in press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about editorial devices, contributors, and the organization of serial publications so readers can judge authorship and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Soliciting Excessive Praise or Historical Exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition can be misapplied — Cicero is criticized for urging Lucceius to 'exceed the Bounds of Truth' in praising him; vanity that pressures others to false praise is censured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pressure critics or historians to amplify praise beyond the truth; maintain honesty in self-promotion and historical record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedications Should Praise Acquired Merits, Not Birth or Fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: In composing a dedication the author will 'not compliment You upon your Birth, Person, or Fortune; nor any other the like Perfections... But shall only touch upon those, which are of your own acquiring, and in which every one must allow You have a real Merit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dedicating a volume, emphasize the dedicatee's cultivated virtues and accomplishments rather than inherited status or material wealth; this yields a more sincere and appropriate dedication.
